questions.stem: What is the structure of a metal?

options.text: Positive ions sharing electrons in pairs
Positive metal ions in a regular arrangement surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons
Alternating positive and negative ions in a lattice
Neutral atoms arranged in layers

questions.explanation: In metallic bonding, metal atoms lose their outer electrons to form positive ions arranged in a regular lattice. The outer electrons become delocalised (free to move) and form a 'sea of electrons' that surrounds and holds together the positive ions. The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the sea of negative electrons is the metallic bond.

questions.stem: Metals can be hammered into shape (they are malleable). Which feature of metallic bonding explains this?

options.text: The covalent bonds between atoms are flexible
Layers of metal ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons continue to hold them together
Metals have weak bonds that break easily
The ions repel each other, allowing movement

questions.explanation: In metals, layers of positive ions can slide over each other when a force is applied. The sea of delocalised electrons moves with the ions and continues to hold the structure together in its new shape. This is unlike ionic compounds where shifting layers causes like charges to align and the structure shatters.

questions.stem: Why do metals generally have high melting points?

options.text: Because metals are very dense
Because the strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons requires a lot of energy to overcome
Because metals have covalent bonds between atoms
Because metal atoms are very large

questions.explanation: The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the regular arrangement of positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these strong attractions throughout the metallic structure, resulting in high melting points. This is not due to covalent bonds or atomic size.

questions.stem: Copper is used for electrical wiring. Which property of metallic bonding makes this possible?

options.text: Copper ions are free to move through the structure
Copper has a high melting point so the wire won't melt
Delocalised electrons can flow through the metal to carry electrical current
Copper is shiny and attractive for wiring

questions.explanation: The delocalised electrons in copper are free to move throughout the metallic structure. When a voltage is applied, these electrons flow in one direction, carrying electrical charge (current). Copper is particularly good because it has a high density of delocalised electrons. The metal ions are fixed in position - it is only the electrons that move.

questions.stem: Iron has a higher melting point than sodium. Using metallic bonding theory, what is the best explanation?

options.text: Iron atoms are heavier than sodium atoms
Iron has more delocalised electrons per atom and a higher ionic charge, creating stronger metallic bonds
Iron is a transition metal and sodium is not
Iron is more dense than sodium

questions.explanation: Iron can lose more outer electrons (typically 2 or 3) than sodium (which loses 1), creating ions with higher charges and contributing more delocalised electrons to the electron sea. The stronger electrostatic attraction between the higher-charged ions and the greater number of delocalised electrons results in stronger metallic bonding and a higher melting point.
